title: What is 1Claw
summary: 1Claw is an HSM-backed, zero-trust vault that lets humans store secrets and lets AI agents fetch only what they're allowed to at runtime.

blocks.text: 1Claw solves a specific problem: your API keys, tokens, and private keys end up pasted into .env files, prompts, and CI configs where anything can read them. 1Claw stores them in HSM-backed vaults instead, and hands them out only to principals a human explicitly allowed.

items: HSM-backed: each vault's key encryption key lives in a hardware security module
Zero-trust: an agent gets zero secrets until a human writes a policy
Two principals: humans own secrets, agents fetch them at runtime
Same API for both at https://api.1claw.co

blocks.text: Humans authenticate with email/password, Google, passkey, or a personal API key (1ck_). Agents authenticate with an agent API key (ocv_) that they trade for a short-lived JWT.

steps.text: Sign up for a free account at the dashboard. The free tier gives you 1,000 requests/month, 3 vaults, and 2 agents.

Get a personal API key from Settings → API Keys. It starts with 1ck_. Export it so the next commands can use it. Replace 1ck_your_key_here with the key you copied from the dashboard at Settings → API Keys.
Verify the key works by exchanging it for an access token against the real API. You'll get back an access_token you can use as a Bearer token.

blocks.text: You now have a verified 1Claw account and a working API key. That's the credential every other lesson builds on.

quiz.question: What backs the encryption key for each 1Claw vault?
options: A password in a config file
quiz.explanation: Each vault has its own HSM-backed key encryption key.

quiz.question: By default, how much access does a new agent have?
options: Access to all secrets tagged public
Zero access until a human writes a policy
quiz.explanation: 1Claw is zero-trust: agents get nothing until a human grants specific paths via a policy.

quiz.question: Which prefix identifies a human's personal API key?
quiz.explanation: Human personal API keys start with 1ck_; agent keys start with ocv_.

title: Vaults, Secrets, and Envelope Encryption
summary: Secrets live at slash-separated paths inside vaults, get a new version on every write, and are protected by a per-secret data key wrapped by the vault's HSM key.

blocks.text: A vault is a container for secrets. A secret is a value stored at a path like api-keys/openai. Every time you write to a path, 1Claw keeps the old value and bumps the version, so you always have history.

items: Vault: isolated container, has its own HSM key encryption key (KEK)
Secret: value at a slash-separated path (api-keys/stripe, passwords/db)
Version: every write creates a new version, newest wins on read
Types: api_key, password, private_key, certificate, ssh_key, note, env_bundle

blocks.text: Envelope encryption: each secret is encrypted with its own random data encryption key (DEK). That DEK is then wrapped by the vault's KEK, which lives in the HSM. The plaintext DEK never sits at rest.

steps.text: Reuse the key you exported in Lesson 1. If it's still in your shell, skip this step.
Get an access token and save it as TOKEN.
Create a vault and auto-extract the vault ID. Requires jq (brew install jq or apt install jq).
steps.code:
export VAULT_ID=$(curl -s -X POST https://api.1claw.co/v1/vaults \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"name":"My Vault","description":"Secrets for my app"}' | jq -r .id)
echo "VAULT_ID=$VAULT_ID"

steps.text: Store a secret at a path inside that vault.
Read it back. The response includes the decrypted value plus metadata like version.

blocks.text: You've now created a vault, written a secret to a path, and read the decrypted value back. That round trip is the whole 1Claw data model in action.

quiz.question: How are secrets addressed inside a vault?
quiz.explanation: Secrets live at slash-separated paths within a vault.

quiz.question: In envelope encryption, what wraps the per-secret data encryption key (DEK)?
options: The vault's HSM-backed key encryption key (KEK)
quiz.explanation: Each secret's DEK is wrapped by the vault KEK, which lives in the HSM.

quiz.question: What happens when you PUT a new value to an existing secret path?
options: It creates a new version and keeps the old one in history
It errors because the path exists
It overwrites and deletes the old value
quiz.explanation: Every write creates a new version; previous versions stay in history.

title: Humans vs Agents
summary: 1Claw has two principal types: humans who own secrets with 1ck_ keys, and agents who trade an ocv_ key for a short-lived JWT and see only what a policy allows.

blocks.text: There are two kinds of principal. Humans create vaults, store secrets, and write policies. Agents are AI assistants or automations that fetch secrets at runtime. Same base URL, same endpoints; only the way you authenticate and what you're allowed to see differ.

items: Human key prefix: 1ck_ (personal API key). It works directly as a Bearer token, or you can exchange it at POST /v1/auth/api-key-token.
Agent key prefix: ocv_ (agent API key). Exchange it at POST /v1/auth/agent-token, sending BOTH agent_id and api_key.
Do not mix them. A 1ck_ key on the agent-token endpoint, a missing agent_id, or an empty variable all return 401 Invalid credentials.
Agent JWTs are short-lived (about 1 hour). Refresh by exchanging the key again.
An agent with a key but no policy sees zero secrets.

blocks.text: Match the key to the endpoint. A 1ck_ human key uses api-key-token (or works as a Bearer token directly). An ocv_ agent key uses agent-token and needs both agent_id and api_key. The wrong key, the wrong endpoint, or an empty shell variable all return the same 401 Invalid credentials, so check those first.

steps.text: Human path. Your 1ck_ key is already a Bearer token, so you can call the API with no exchange step.
Prefer a short-lived JWT for the human key? Exchange it at the api-key-token endpoint. This is a different endpoint from the agent one.

Agent path. First, create an agent using your human 1ck_ key. Use the VAULT_ID from Lesson 2, or copy a vault id from the Step 1 response. Export it if not already set. The response contains the agent_id and a plaintext api_key (starts with ocv_). Save both: the ocv_ key is shown only once.
steps.code:
# Make sure VAULT_ID is set (from Lesson 2 or Step 1 above)
export VAULT_ID="your-vault-uuid-here"

AGENT_RESPONSE=$(curl -s -X POST https://api.1claw.co/v1/agents \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $ONECLAW_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d "{\"name\":\"my-first-agent\",\"token_ttl_seconds\":3600,\"vault_ids\":[\"$VAULT_ID\"]}")
echo "$AGENT_RESPONSE"

steps.text: Extract agent_id and api_key from the response above. The ocv_ key is shown only at creation time: save it somewhere safe.
Exchange the agent credentials for a short-lived JWT. Send agent_id AND api_key. Both are required. Capture the token for the next step.
steps.code:
export AGENT_TOKEN=$(curl -s -X POST https://api.1claw.co/v1/auth/agent-token \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d "{\"agent_id\":\"$ONECLAW_AGENT_ID\",\"api_key\":\"$ONECLAW_AGENT_KEY\"}" | jq -r .access_token)
echo "AGENT_TOKEN=$AGENT_TOKEN"

steps.text: Verify the token works by calling the agents/me endpoint. You should see the agent's metadata.
Both paths give you a Bearer credential. Use it on the same secret endpoints. The agent only sees what a policy has granted.

blocks.text: You've authenticated both ways: a human 1ck_ key used as a Bearer token, and an agent ocv_ key exchanged (with its agent_id) for a JWT. Same API, different door.

quiz.question: Which prefix marks an agent API key?
quiz.explanation: Agent API keys start with ocv_; human personal keys start with 1ck_.

quiz.question: How does an agent turn its ocv_ key into a usable API credential?
options: Emails it to the human each time
POSTs agent_id and api_key to /v1/auth/agent-token for a short-lived JWT
Uses it directly as a permanent password
quiz.explanation: The agent-token endpoint needs both agent_id and api_key; api-key-token is the human 1ck_ path.

quiz.question: What happens to an agent's active tokens when a human changes its policy?
options: They're automatically revoked and must be re-exchanged
quiz.explanation: Policy create/update/delete auto-revokes the agent's active JWTs, forcing a fresh exchange.

concepts.note: why an agent is not just another service account

title: Install the CLI
summary: Install @1claw/cli, log in with the browser device flow, and confirm access with whoami and vault list.

blocks.text: The CLI is the fastest way to work with 1Claw from a terminal. Install it, log in, and you'll have a working authenticated session in under a minute.
Prerequisite: Node 20+ if you install via npm. Homebrew works on macOS and Linux and needs nothing else.

What `1claw setup` does under the hood: it calls POST /v1/onboarding/provision, which creates the welcome bundle (a `default` vault, `examples/hello`, an MCP agent, and a `**` read/write policy) and returns a one-time `ocv_` agent key plus a ready-to-paste `mcp_stdio_config`. Track progress any time with GET /v1/org/onboarding/status. The manual steps below are the same thing, done by hand.

steps.text: Fastest path: one command. `1claw setup` provisions a `default` vault, an `examples/hello` secret, an MCP agent, and a read/write policy, then writes MCP config for Cursor, Claude Desktop, and VS Code. Run it and skip to the last step.
Install the CLI with npm (needs Node 20+) or Homebrew.
Log in. This opens your browser to 1claw.co, you approve, and the CLI polls until you confirm. No password typed in the terminal.
Confirm who you're logged in as.
List your vaults to prove the session reaches the API.

blocks.text: If you already exported ONECLAW_API_KEY in Lesson 1, you can skip browser login and use that key instead (see the CI tip below).
For CI or any non-interactive shell, skip login and set env vars instead: export ONECLAW_TOKEN="your-jwt" or export ONECLAW_API_KEY="1ck_..." (add ONECLAW_VAULT_ID for vault-scoped commands).
The CLI is installed and authenticated. 1claw whoami and 1claw vault list both work, so you're ready to create vaults and secrets from the terminal.

quiz.question: What Node version does the npm install of the CLI require?
quiz.explanation: npm install -g @1claw/cli requires Node 20 or newer.

quiz.question: What does 1claw login use so you never type a password in the terminal?
quiz.explanation: 1claw login opens the browser, you approve there, and the CLI polls until confirmed.

quiz.question: Which env var lets the CLI run non-interactively with a personal API key in CI?
quiz.explanation: Set ONECLAW_API_KEY (or ONECLAW_TOKEN) to skip interactive login.

title: Start local: a vault with no account
summary: Encrypt secrets on your own machine with 1claw local, before you sign up for anything.

blocks.text: You do not need an account, a network, or a credit card to get value from 1Claw. The CLI ships a local encrypted vault that works entirely offline, and it is the right place for a developer to start: it solves the .env-file problem on your own laptop first, and everything you learn transfers to the hosted vault later.

items: The vault is a single encrypted file at ~/.config/1claw/local-vault.enc.
It is AES-256-GCM, with the key derived from your passphrase by scrypt.
The file is written with 0600 permissions, so only your user can read it.
Nothing leaves your machine unless you explicitly run a sync.

steps.text: Create the vault. You will be prompted for a passphrase twice; it must be at least 8 characters.
Add a secret. You are prompted for the value rather than passing it as an argument, which keeps it out of your shell history.
List what is stored. Names only, never values.
Read one back.
steps.code:
1claw local get stripe/test-key

# or masked, when someone is looking over your shoulder
1claw local get stripe/test-key --masked

steps.text: Check the vault's state at any time.
Remove a secret you no longer need.

blocks.text: Unlocking is deliberately slow. scrypt is configured with a large work factor, so each command takes a moment while it derives the key. That cost is what makes a stolen vault file expensive to brute force.

The passphrase cannot be recovered. There is no reset, no support path, and no escrow: if you forget it, the only option is `1claw local destroy`, which deletes the vault so you can start over. Put the passphrase in your password manager before you add anything you care about.

This is the whole local story, and for a solo developer it may be all you ever need. The next two lessons cover the two things it cannot do: share a secret with a teammate, and give an agent scoped access. Both are what the hosted vault is for.

quiz.question: Where does the local vault store its data?
options: In a single encrypted file at ~/.config/1claw/local-vault.enc
In a hidden folder in the current project
quiz.explanation: It is one AES-256-GCM file written with 0600 permissions. Nothing is transmitted anywhere until you explicitly run a sync.

quiz.question: You forget your local vault passphrase. What are your options?
options: Reset it with your account email
None; the only path is `1claw local destroy` and starting over
Support can decrypt it with the master key
quiz.explanation: The passphrase is the only key material and it is never stored. destroy exists precisely because deletion is the only available recovery, which is why the passphrase belongs in a password manager.

quiz.question: Why does each local command take a noticeable moment?
options: scrypt derives the key with a large work factor, which is what makes brute forcing the file expensive
It checks for updates over the network
It verifies the file against a remote checksum
It re-encrypts the whole vault on every read
quiz.explanation: The delay is the security property. A fast key derivation would make an offline attack against a stolen vault file cheap.

title: Bring your existing .env
summary: Import the .env files you already have, then export them back on demand so your tooling never changes.

blocks.text: Nobody starts from an empty vault. You start with a handful of .env files scattered across projects, which is the exact problem worth solving, so the local vault imports them directly.

steps.text: Look before you leap. A dry run shows what would be imported without writing anything.
Import for real. Existing entries are skipped rather than overwritten unless you say otherwise.
If you do want to overwrite what is already there, be explicit about it.
Export back to .env format when a tool needs a file. Without -o it writes to stdout, so you can pipe it.
steps.code:
1claw local export

# or straight to a file your tooling expects
1claw local export -o .env

blocks.text: Once a secret is in the vault, delete the .env from the project and add it to .gitignore. Importing without removing the original leaves you with two copies and no improvement.

The import and export pair is deliberately boring, and that is the point: it means adopting the vault does not require changing how any of your tools work. You keep the .env-shaped interface at the edges and stop keeping plaintext files around between runs.
`1claw env run -- <command>` goes one step further: it resolves the values and injects them into a child process's environment, so nothing is ever written to disk at all.

quiz.question: What does `1claw local import .env --dry-run` do?
options: Imports only the keys that do not already exist
Shows what would be imported without writing anything
Imports into a temporary vault for testing
quiz.explanation: It is a preview. Running it first is worth the habit on any file you have not read recently.

quiz.question: By default, what happens to a key that already exists in the vault?
options: It is skipped, unless you pass --force
Both values are kept as separate versions
The import aborts with an error
It is overwritten with the .env value
quiz.explanation: Skipping is the safe default, since the vault copy is more likely to be current than a file that has been sitting in a project directory.

quiz.question: What should you do with the .env file after importing it?
options: Encrypt it with the same passphrase
Move it to a shared drive
Delete it and add it to .gitignore, or the import achieved nothing
quiz.explanation: Two copies is the sprawl problem the vault exists to remove. The value only improves once the plaintext original is gone.

title: Your First Vault and Secret
summary: Use the CLI to create a vault, store a secret, and read it back, with the dashboard as an alternative.

blocks.text: Now that the CLI is authenticated, storing and reading a secret is three commands. This is the everyday human workflow.

steps.text: Confirm you're logged in (from the install lesson).
Create a vault. The command prints the new vault's id.

Export the vault ID from the create output so subsequent commands target this vault. If you already created a vault in Lesson 2, you can reuse it: run 1claw vault list and export that vault's UUID instead of creating a new one.
Store a secret at a path. Give it a type so 1Claw knows what it is. The CLI uses ONECLAW_VAULT_ID to pick the vault.
Read the value back.
List the secrets in the vault (metadata only, never values).

blocks.text: Prefer clicking? In the dashboard at 1claw.co, go to Vaults then Create vault, then Secrets then Add secret at a path like api-keys/openai. It hits the same endpoints as the CLI.
You have a real vault with a stored secret you can read on demand. From here you can grant an agent access or wire secrets into your app.

quiz.question: Which CLI command stores a secret at a path?
quiz.explanation: 1claw secret set <path> --value ... --type ... stores a secret.

quiz.question: What does 1claw secret list return?
quiz.explanation: Listing returns paths, types, and versions but never the secret values.

quiz.question: The dashboard is best described as what?
options: A UI on top of the same API endpoints the CLI uses
quiz.explanation: The dashboard at 1claw.co is a web UI over the same endpoints.

concepts.note: what happens to the value at rest

title: From local to cloud
summary: Push your local vault to a hosted one when you need a second person, a second machine, or an agent.

blocks.text: The local vault has exactly three limits, and you hit them in a predictable order: you get a second machine, then a teammate, then an agent. All three need a vault that exists somewhere other than your laptop.

items: A second machine needs the secret to exist off your disk.
A teammate needs sharing, access control and an audit trail.
An agent needs a scoped identity, which is the whole rest of this course.

blocks.text: Requires: a 1Claw account and a cloud vault. `npx @1claw/cli setup` creates one along with everything else in a single command.

steps.text: Log in. The browser flow means no password is typed into your terminal.
Preview the move. Push is the default direction: local to cloud.
Pull instead, to seed a fresh laptop from a vault that already exists.
Conflicts are skipped by default. Overwrite only when you are sure which side is authoritative.
Confirm the cloud side has what you expect.

blocks.text: Sync skips conflicts rather than guessing. That is the right default and it means a sync can silently do less than you assumed, so read the summary rather than trusting the exit code.

Keeping the local vault after syncing is a reasonable choice. It works offline, it survives an outage, and it costs nothing. What changes is that the cloud vault becomes the authoritative copy once more than one person or machine depends on it.

From here the course is about the things only a hosted vault can do: policies that scope access per principal, agents as first-class identities with short-lived tokens, execution without ever handing over a credential, and an audit trail that answers who read what. The local vault got you started without a signup; the rest of this course is why teams outgrow it.

quiz.question: Which direction does `1claw local sync` move secrets by default?
options: It prompts for a direction each time
quiz.explanation: Push is the default because the common first case is seeding a hosted vault from the laptop where the secrets already are.

quiz.question: What happens by default when a secret exists on both sides with different values?
options: The conflict is skipped unless you pass --force
quiz.explanation: Skipping avoids silently destroying a value. It also means a sync can do less than you expected, so the summary is worth reading.

quiz.question: What is the first thing the local vault cannot give you?
options: A secret that exists anywhere other than your own disk
quiz.explanation: Local encryption is genuinely good. The limits are all about existing in more than one place: a second machine, a teammate, or an agent.
